summary: Phonics practice that follows the class.
description: Teachers choose the sounds already taught. Children practise blending, then read short decodable sentences using those sounds.
purpose: Read an unfamiliar word independently using taught sound–letter relationships.
application: A short literacy rotation, with the same sound set available for practice at home.
peer: Fast Phonics offers sequenced synthetic phonics lessons.
value: The proposed draw: teachers set the sequence, so practice stays in step with this week’s teaching. Parents get a clear starting point.
lesson: Read a new word on paper
validation: Test whether sound-set setup is quick enough for weekly use, and whether children transfer the skill to unseen words.
route: Trial with early years teams; test a school licence with teacher-directed home practice.

sources.name: Fast Phonics
sources.fact: Describes sequenced lessons using systematic synthetic phonics, reinforcing classroom learning.

summary: Show the thinking behind the answer.
description: Students combine drawing, movement and voice to explain how something works. Teachers set a challenge and review the explanation.
purpose: Explain cause and effect, then predict what happens when one part changes.
application: A quick check of understanding in science, maths or humanities.
peer: Explain Everything already combines whiteboarding and recorded explanations.
value: A focused explanation task could make reasoning easier to assess. The opportunity is useful prompts and review, in a well-served creation category.
validation: Compare teacher review time and the misconceptions found against a normal whiteboard recording task.
route: Pilot one subject unit with a teaching team before testing a cross-subject school licence.

sources.name: Explain Everything
sources.fact: Students can record screencasts of their understanding and collaborate on digital whiteboards.

reason: I find Explain Everything too expensive. I want to offer teachers and schools a more affordable way to create and assess explanations.

summary: Make a decision. Make the case.
description: Students weigh community proposals, hear different views and work within a budget in a simulated council or parliament.
purpose: Defend a feasible civic decision with evidence, costs and an explicit trade-off.
application: A small-group council simulation inside a civics inquiry.
peer: iCivics’ Counties Work explores local services, budgets and citizens’ needs.
value: Australian civic scenarios and a visible decision trail could give teachers a ready-to-run discussion with assessable reasoning.
validation: Check local curriculum relevance, preparation time and whether students justify a trade-off rather than simply vote.
route: Start with a civics unit pack; test repeat use and willingness to buy further scenarios.

sources.name: iCivics: Counties Work
sources.fact: Players run a county; learning objectives cover government responsibilities and the effects of budgets and revenue on services and citizens.

reason: I think civics is underserved by learning apps. There’s room for a substantial library of scenarios, issues and decisions that students can keep coming back to.

summary: Turn a school walk into an investigation.
description: Students record biodiversity, weather and water observations, compare evidence and bring their findings back to class.
purpose: Make a comparison from consistent observations and explain what the evidence cannot establish.
application: A field record for an outdoor science lesson or a longer local inquiry.
peer: Seek identifies living things and offers observation challenges.
value: The proposed focus is the whole investigation: a shared method, comparable records and a classroom explanation across several science topics.
validation: Test whether students collect comparable data and whether teachers can manage the outdoor-to-classroom transition easily.
route: Pilot a school-ground science unit; assess repeat use across weather, water and habitat topics.

sources.name: Seek by iNaturalist
sources.fact: Uses image recognition to identify organisms, with badges and observation challenges.

reason: I feel we’re losing the field-notebook habit. I want to bring it into the digital age, getting students outside to observe, record and explore science in real places.

summary: Practise the thinking behind a fair test.
description: Students choose variables, predict outcomes and interpret virtual experiments when a physical investigation is impractical.
purpose: Control variables and use results to support or revise a prediction.
application: Preparation for a practical, or an investigation when equipment is unavailable.
peer: PhET and Gizmos already support inquiry through interactive simulations.
value: A consistent plan–test–explain routine could make scientific reasoning easier to review. It needs a clear workflow advantage over strong existing options.
validation: Compare preparation and assessment effort with a PhET or Gizmos lesson; check transfer to a physical experiment.
route: Pilot a small investigation set with science departments before expanding the simulation library.

sources.name: PhET
sources.fact: Provides simulations and classroom facilitation strategies for inquiry.

sources.name: ExploreLearning Gizmos
sources.fact: Describes inquiry-based virtual labs where students can repeat experiments and investigate concepts.

reason: Physical experiments aren’t always practical or possible. I want to make them accessible through clear visual simulations, giving schools more ways to run meaningful science lessons.

summary: A good reason to use fractions.
description: Students resize recipes, share portions and measure quantities in a virtual kitchen. Teachers choose the maths and difficulty.
purpose: Find an unknown quantity, explain a valid strategy and check the result.
application: A maths rotation that connects to measuring, sharing or cooking off-screen.
peer: Osmo Pizza Co. combines food play with arithmetic, fractions and money.
value: Teacher-selected recipe problems and visible working could connect screen practice with everyday maths. No specialist play kit is proposed.
validation: Test whether students explain the operation and apply it to a different recipe without prompts.
route: Trial with primary maths teams; separately test parent interest in optional home challenges.

sources.name: Osmo Pizza Co.
sources.fact: Combines tangible play pieces with a pizza business game covering addition, subtraction and fractions.

summary: Tell it. Hear it. Tell it more clearly.
description: Children arrange pictures, record a story and listen back. They improve one part before saving another telling in a private classroom collection.
purpose: Tell a connected oral story and revise a part a listener finds unclear.
application: Early oral-language practice, including English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D).
peer: Book Creator supports picture prompts, voice recording and language practice.
value: A short, repeatable retelling routine could make oral-language progress easier to hear. The value would be the teaching flow and comparison between attempts.
validation: Compare clarity between tellings and teacher review effort; test use with multilingual learners without judging accent as ability.
route: Pilot in early years and EAL/D groups, then test a class licence around repeat recording routines.

sources.name: Book Creator
sources.fact: Provides speaking and listening templates, including picture description and voice recording.

reason: Children often have more to say than they can write. I want to give them space to practise storytelling and hear their own progress.

summary: Build a map someone else can use.
description: Students map classrooms, islands and neighbourhoods with symbols, directions and simple scale, then exchange navigation challenges.
purpose: Make a consistent map, communicate a route and explain a placement decision.
application: A geography making task that starts with a school walk and ends with a partner test.
peer: National Geographic MapMaker offers interactive maps, sketching and geography activities.
value: A small, familiar place gives younger learners a focused start. Teachers get evidence through whether another child can actually use the map.
validation: Test independent map use across the wide year range; compare with paper maps and existing mapping tools.
route: Begin with lower-primary map skills; validate advanced scale tasks separately before serving the full year range.

sources.name: National Geographic MapMaker
sources.fact: Offers curated maps and activities, 2D/3D exploration, sketching and custom maps for students.

reason: I want children to understand maps by making places and testing directions with someone else.

summary: An answer is better with a clue.
description: Students investigate illustrated stories, choose clues from the text and explain motives, predictions or apparent contradictions.
purpose: Support a plausible inference with relevant text evidence and explain the connection.
application: A guided reading task with spoken, drawn or written reasoning.
peer: ReadTheory adapts comprehension passages and questions to a learner’s reading level.
value: The proposed draw is seeing why a child chose an answer. Flexible response modes could make reasoning easier to assess when writing is a barrier.
validation: Check whether explanations reveal misconceptions and whether the review workload is manageable in a normal reading group.
route: Pilot one reading group, then test a school literacy licence if teachers use the evidence to plan follow-up teaching.

sources.name: ReadTheory
sources.fact: Describes adaptive reading comprehension that matches texts and questions to each student’s reading level.

reason: A correct answer doesn’t always reveal understanding. I want students to show which clues shaped their thinking.

summary: Try seeing it from the other side.
description: Short school stories let children explore different perspectives and possible responses, with a teacher guiding the conversation.
purpose: Consider two viewpoints, compare likely consequences and explain a constructive response.
application: A class discussion or small-group role-play, with room for several reasonable answers.
peer: Everyday Speech offers illustrated scenarios and perspective-taking activities.
value: Short, locally familiar stories could make discussion easier to start. Open responses and teacher facilitation are central to the proposed value.
validation: Check that children can explain both perspectives; co-design with diverse learners and test teacher confidence facilitating discussion.
route: Pilot through classroom and wellbeing teams; assess repeat use without positioning it as therapy or a behaviour score.

sources.name: Everyday Speech
sources.fact: Offers illustrated school scenarios with prompts for discussing feelings and perspectives in elementary settings.

reason: Everyday disagreements offer useful learning opportunities. I want children to explore different perspectives without being pushed towards one supposedly correct response.

description: A character follows students’ directions exactly. Missing steps and vague wording create visible problems that students fix and retest.
purpose: Write an ordered, precise procedure and revise it using evidence from a failed attempt.
application: Procedural writing practice with an immediate reason to edit.
peer: Code.org’s maze tasks teach ordered commands through block-based movement.
value: The proposed focus is everyday language: make the sentence clear enough for someone to act on. That gives English teachers a concrete revision task.
validation: Test whether interpretation is predictable and feedback is fair; check transfer to real written instructions.
route: Start with tightly scoped procedural-writing challenges and teacher trials before expanding the language the character understands.

sources.name: Code.org: Maze sequence
sources.fact: Students order movement commands as sequential steps in a program using a block-based maze activity.

summary: One small edit. A clearer piece of writing.
description: Teachers set one revision goal. Students improve their own draft, compare versions and explain what changed for the reader.
purpose: Make a purposeful revision that preserves meaning and improves clarity.
application: A focused step between a first draft and a teacher or peer conference.
peer: Quill offers short writing exercises with immediate feedback and repeated revision.
value: Working on the child’s own draft, one goal at a time, could make teacher feedback easier to act on and improvement easier to discuss.
validation: Check independent use of the revision move in later writing and whether teachers spend less time repeating the same feedback.
route: Trial during an existing writing unit; test a team licence if it becomes part of the regular feedback routine.

sources.name: Quill
sources.fact: Provides supplemental writing exercises in short sessions, with feedback and opportunities to revise sentences.
